```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(knapsack)   # replace with your package name if different
```

## Introduction

This vignette answers four questions about the knapsack algorithms in this
package. The package offers four ways to solve the problem, where every item
has a weight `w` and a value `v`, and the goal is to maximize total value
without exceeding the weight limit `W`:

| Function | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `brute_force_knapsack()` | Checks all $2^n$ combinations | Exact |
| `knapsack_dynamic()` | Dynamic programming, $O(nW)$ | Exact |
| `knapsack_greedy()` | Sorts by value/weight ratio | Approximate |
| `brute_force_knapsack_parallel(..., parallel = TRUE)` | Brute force split across CPU cores | Exact |

All timings below are measured with `system.time()` while this vignette is
built, so the exact numbers depend on the machine.

## Test data

We generate a reproducible data set of 1,000,000 candidate objects. Smaller
problems take the first `n` rows of it.

```{r data}
suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
head(knapsack_objects)
```

## Question 1: How long does brute force take for n = 16 objects?

```{r brute16}
items16 <- knapsack_objects[1:16, ]

time_brute16 <- system.time(
  res_brute16 <- brute_force_knapsack(items16, W = 3500)
)

res_brute16
time_brute16
```

Brute force with 16 objects evaluates $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ combinations and
took **`r round(time_brute16[["elapsed"]], 2)` seconds** here.

The cost doubles with every extra object, so 20 objects would need roughly 16
times as long and 25 objects (the limit enforced by the function) roughly 512
times as long.

## Question 2: How long does dynamic programming take for n = 500 objects?

```{r dynamic500}
items500 <- knapsack_objects[1:500, ]

time_dyn500 <- system.time(
  res_dyn500 <- knapsack_dynamic(items500, W = 3500)
)

res_dyn500$value
length(res_dyn500$elements)
time_dyn500
```

Dynamic programming with 500 objects and capacity 3500 took
**`r round(time_dyn500[["elapsed"]], 2)` seconds**. Its running time grows
with $n \times W$ instead of $2^n$, which is why 500 objects is no problem
while brute force is impossible at that size. The price is that the time (and
the memory for the table) also grows with the capacity `W`, which must be an
integer.

## Question 3: How long does the greedy heuristic take for n = 1,000,000 objects?

```{r data-big}
suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n_big <- 1000000
knapsack_big <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n_big, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n_big, 0, 10000)
)
```

```{r greedy1e6}
time_greedy <- system.time(
  res_greedy <- knapsack_greedy(knapsack_big, W = 3500)
)

res_greedy$value
length(res_greedy$elements)
time_greedy
```

The greedy heuristic handled all 1,000,000 objects in
**`r round(time_greedy[["elapsed"]], 2)` seconds**. Its cost is dominated by
sorting the value/weight ratios, $O(n \log n)$. The trade-off is that it does
not always find the optimal value. We can check how close it gets on the
500-object problem, where the exact answer is known:

```{r greedy-quality}
res_greedy500 <- knapsack_greedy(items500, W = 3500)
round(res_greedy500$value / res_dyn500$value * 100, 2)
```

On this instance, the greedy solution reaches
**`r round(res_greedy500$value / res_dyn500$value * 100, 2)`%** of the optimal
value.

## Question 4: What performance gain can parallelizing brute force give?

Brute force is well suited to parallelization because the combinations are
independent: the search space is split into equal chunks, each CPU core
searches one chunk, and the best result from all workers is kept.

The calls look like this:

```{r parallel-small}
# items <- data.frame(
#   w = c(2, 3, 4),
#   v = c(3, 4, 5)
# )
items <- knapsack_objects[1:16, ]

sequential <- brute_force_knapsack(items, W = 5)
parallel_result <- brute_force_knapsack_parallel(
  items, W = 5, parallel = TRUE
)

sequential
parallel_result
```

Both return the same solution. Now we compare the running time on larger
problems, where there is enough work to make the parallel version worthwhile.

```{r parallel-compare}
compare_timing <- function(n) {
  items <- knapsack_objects[1:n, ]

  t_seq <- system.time(
    res_seq <- brute_force_knapsack(items, W = 3500)
  )[["elapsed"]]

  t_par <- system.time(
    res_par <- brute_force_knapsack_parallel(items, W = 3500, parallel = TRUE)
  )[["elapsed"]]

  data.frame(
    n = n,
    sequential_sec = round(t_seq, 2),
    parallel_sec = round(t_par, 2),
    speedup = round(t_seq / t_par, 2),
    same_result = identical(res_seq$value, res_par$value)
  )
}

timings <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(16, 18, 20), compare_timing))
timings
```

This machine has **`r parallel::detectCores()` logical cores**.

How to read the table:

- **Small n:** the parallel version can be *slower*. Starting the worker
  processes and copying the data to them has a fixed cost of about a second,
  which is larger than the work itself when $n$ is small.
- **Larger n:** the work grows as $2^n$ while the startup cost stays constant,
  so the speedup increases and approaches the number of cores (it will not
  reach it exactly, because of the startup cost and because the chunks
  are combined at the end).

For $n = 20$ the parallel search reached a speedup of
**`r timings$speedup[timings$n == 20]`x** over the sequential one.

## Summary

| Algorithm | Objects | Time (sec) |
|---|---|---|
| Brute force | 16 | `r round(time_brute16[["elapsed"]], 2)` |
| Dynamic programming | 500 | `r round(time_dyn500[["elapsed"]], 2)` |
| Greedy heuristic | 1,000,000 | `r round(time_greedy[["elapsed"]], 2)` |

Brute force and dynamic programming return the optimal solution, but brute
force only works for very small $n$ and dynamic programming needs a moderate,
integer capacity. The greedy heuristic scales to millions of objects but may
return a suboptimal value. Parallelizing brute force helps once the problem is
large enough to outweigh the startup cost, but it cannot overcome the
exponential growth in $n$.
